# 2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election
## 1\. Introduction
The **2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election** was a statewide judicial retention election held on Tuesday, November 4, 2025, in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania . The election determined the tenure of three incumbent justices of the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania: Justice Christine Donohue, Justice Kevin Dougherty, and Justice David Wecht. All three jurists, who were originally elected in a historic Democratic sweep in 2015, sought retention for a second ten-year term .

This election cycle was notable for the unusually high level of politicization, campaign spending, and strategic attention directed toward what is typically a low-profile judicial retention process . While retention elections in Pennsylvania are nonpartisan in format—voters are presented with a simple "Yes" or "No" question regarding each justice—the 2025 contest functioned effectively as a partisan proxy war . The retention of the three justices was critical for the Democratic Party to maintain its 5–2 majority on the state's highest court, a dominance established during the 2015 election . Conversely, Republican-aligned interest groups and conservative donors viewed the election as a rare opportunity to alter the ideological trajectory of the court, which had issued pivotal rulings on congressional redistricting, voting rights, and reproductive healthcare in the preceding decade .

The campaign was characterized by unprecedented financial expenditures, estimated to exceed $15 million, driven largely by independent expenditure groups and Political Action Committees (PACs) . Pro-retention forces, organizing under banners such as "Pennsylvanians for Judicial Fairness," framed the election as a referendum on the independence of the judiciary and the protection of civil liberties, specifically abortion access following the federal overturning of *Roe v. Wade*.5 Opposition groups, including the "Commonwealth Leaders Fund" and the "Republican State Leadership Committee," mounted a "Vote No" campaign that criticized the justices as "activist judges" responsible for controversial decisions regarding the COVID-19 pandemic and election administration .

On election night, all three justices were retained by decisive margins. Official results certified by the Secretary of the Commonwealth indicated that each justice received approximately 61% to 62% of the affirmative vote . The results were uniform across the three incumbents, suggesting that the electorate largely viewed them as a unified slate . The successful retention ensured the continuation of the Democratic majority on the court until at least 2027, when Justice Donohue is scheduled to retire due to the state's mandatory judicial retirement age .

The election also served as a significant bellwether for the shifting political geography of Pennsylvania. Democratic incumbents performed strongly in traditional swing counties such as Erie and Northampton, outperforming the top-of-ticket metrics from the previous year's presidential election . This divergence highlighted the distinct dynamics of judicial retention elections, where the power of incumbency and the specific framing of judicial independence can often transcend the stark partisan polarization seen in executive and legislative races .

## 2\. Background
### 2.1. The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania
The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania is the court of last resort for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. It claims the distinction of being the oldest appellate court in the United States, predating the United States Supreme Court by several decades . The court consists of seven justices who are elected to ten-year terms. The court exercises plenary jurisdiction over the state's legal system and has the final authority on matters of Pennsylvania law and the state constitution .

Because the court has the power to interpret the state constitution, its composition is of immense political consequence. In the years leading up to the 2025 election, the court played a central role in resolving disputes between the Democratic executive branch (under Governors Tom Wolf and Josh Shapiro) and the Republican-controlled General Assembly . These disputes frequently involved high-stakes issues such as the drawing of congressional and legislative district maps, the legality of mail-in voting procedures, and the scope of the governor's emergency powers during the COVID-19 pandemic .

### 2.2. Judicial Selection and Retention
Pennsylvania utilizes a hybrid system for judicial selection that combines partisan elections with merit retention.

* **Initial Election:** Justices are initially selected in partisan statewide elections. Candidates run in party primaries (Democratic and Republican) and then face off in a general election. The winners serve an initial ten-year term . 
* **Retention Election:** At the conclusion of their ten-year term, justices do not face a challenger. Instead, they stand for "retention." Their name appears on the general election ballot with a nonpartisan question: "Shall \[Justice Name\] be retained for an additional term as Justice of the Supreme Court of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania?" Voters must choose "Yes" or "No" .

If a justice receives more than 50% "Yes" votes, they are retained for another ten-year term. If they receive more "No" votes than "Yes" votes, their seat is declared vacant. The Governor must then appoint a replacement, subject to confirmation by two-thirds of the State Senate, to serve until the next municipal election, at which point a partisan election is held to fill the seat permanently .

Historically, retention elections in Pennsylvania have been low-maintenance affairs for incumbents. Since the modern retention system was established by the Constitutional Convention of 1968, only one Supreme Court justice has ever lost a retention vote: Justice Russell Nigro in 2005 . Nigro's defeat was the result of a unique public backlash against a legislative pay raise that the court had allowed to stand, an event that galvanized a bipartisan "Vote No" movement . Apart from that singular event, retention rates for appellate judges in Pennsylvania hover near 98%, with most justices securing retention with little campaign activity .

However, the political climate of the 2020s introduced new volatility to this system. The increasing nationalization of state supreme court races, driven by the U.S. Supreme Court's devolution of major policy questions (such as abortion and gerrymandering) to the state level, transformed retention elections into potential battlegrounds .

### 2.3. The 2015 "Democratic Sweep"
The political stakes of the 2025 election were directly rooted in the outcome of the 2015 Pennsylvania Supreme Court election. In 2015, due to a series of resignations and retirements, three seats on the seven-member court were open simultaneously—an unprecedented occurrence in modern state history . The Democratic Party nominated three candidates: Superior Court Judges Christine Donohue and David Wecht, and Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas Judge Kevin Dougherty.

The Democrats won all three seats in a "sweep," flipping the partisan control of the court from Republican to Democratic . This victory established the 5–2 Democratic majority that would define the court's jurisprudence for the next decade. The 2025 retention election was the first time these three justices faced voters since that pivotal victory. For Republicans, 2025 represented the first major opportunity to chip away at the majority that had been established ten years prior .

## 3\. The Incumbents
The three justices seeking retention in 2025—Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht—shared a party background but possessed distinct judicial records and personal narratives.

### 3.1. Justice Christine Donohue
**Christine Donohue** served on the Superior Court of Pennsylvania for eight years prior to her election to the Supreme Court in 2015 . A native of Pennsylvania with a background in private practice, she was often viewed as a pragmatic voice on the bench.

* **Judicial Tenure:** During her first term, Donohue authored several significant opinions and was part of the majority in key civil rights cases. Her supporters highlighted her role in protecting reproductive rights; although the court had not yet issued a definitive ruling on the state constitution's protection of abortion rights by 2025, Donohue was featured in advertisements linking her retention to the defense of such rights . 
* **Evaluation:** The Pennsylvania Bar Association (PBA) Judicial Evaluation Commission recommended her for retention, describing her as "thorough and well-prepared for oral arguments," "smart and fair," and "attentive and engaged" . 
* **Term Limitations:** A unique factor in Donohue's retention was her age. Under Pennsylvania law, judges must retire at the end of the calendar year in which they turn 75\. Donohue was expected to reach this mandatory retirement age in 2027, meaning that her retention vote in 2025 was effectively for a two-year extension rather than a full decade. This fact was noted by political observers but did not become a central theme of the opposition campaign .

### 3.2. Justice Kevin Dougherty
**Kevin M. Dougherty** brought a different profile to the high court. Before 2015, he was the Administrative Judge of the Family Division of the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas . He was widely known in state politics not only for his judicial service but also for his family; he is the brother of John "Johnny Doc" Dougherty, a prominent and powerful Philadelphia labor leader who was convicted on federal corruption charges in the years preceding the 2025 election .

* **Separation from Family Controversy:** Despite his brother's legal troubles, Justice Dougherty successfully maintained a distinct professional identity. He was not implicated in his brother's activities, and he continued to receive broad support from the legal community and labor unions . His son, Sean Dougherty, also served as a member of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, further cementing the family's political footprint . 
* **Judicial Style:** The PBA recommended Dougherty for retention, noting that attorneys described him as "attentive, smart, well prepared" and "open to consideration of differing perspectives" . His background in family court often informed his perspective on cases involving juvenile justice and social services. 
* **Campaign Performance:** Dougherty was a robust fundraiser, raising over $2.6 million for his retention committee—significantly more than his colleagues .

### 3.3. Justice David Wecht
**David N. Wecht** served on the Pennsylvania Superior Court before joining the Supreme Court. He is the son of the famous forensic pathologist Cyril Wecht, a connection that gave him high name recognition in Western Pennsylvania .

* **Jurisprudence:** Wecht is known for his scholarly, lengthy, and often forceful opinions. He frequently writes concurrences or dissents that explore the historical and theoretical underpinnings of the law . One of his most notable contributions was in the realm of education funding; he authored a majority opinion asserting that petitioners had the right to challenge the state's education funding formula under the constitution, a ruling that paved the way for the landmark *William Penn* decision which declared the state's school funding system unconstitutional . 
* **Target of Opposition:** Because of his outspoken nature and his authorship of key opinions regarding election administration (such as the extension of mail-in ballot deadlines in 2020), Wecht was a primary target for conservative opposition groups. The "Vote No" campaigns frequently featured his image and cited his rulings as examples of "judicial overreach" . 
* **Evaluation:** Despite the partisan attacks, the PBA highly recommended him, stating his opinions were "well written and logical" and his judicial temperament "above reproach" .

## 4\. Campaign Dynamics and Issues
The 2025 retention election transformed into a high-stakes political battleground, deviating from the norm of quiet judicial confirmations. The campaign environment was shaped by the broader national polarization surrounding the judiciary and specific grievances regarding Pennsylvania state policy.

### 4.1. The "Politicization" of Retention
Observers noted that the 2025 cycle was one of the most politicized retention elections in memory . While the ballot itself remained nonpartisan, the external campaign environment was deeply partisan. The structural reality of the court—a 5-2 Democratic majority—meant that the retention election was the only mechanism available to Republicans to disrupt Democratic control before the next scheduled open-seat election .

### 4.2. The "Vote No" Campaign (Opposition)
Conservative groups and the Republican Party infrastructure coalesced around a "Vote No" message. This campaign was driven by several key themes:

* **"Activist Judges":** The core argument was that Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht had acted as "super-legislators" rather than impartial jurists. Opponents cited the court's 2018 decision to strike down the GOP-drawn congressional map as an unconstitutional gerrymander, arguing that the court had usurped the legislature's role . 
* **COVID-19 Policies:** The opposition highlighted the court's rulings that upheld Governor Tom Wolf's emergency powers during the pandemic, including business closures and mask mandates. These decisions were framed as "lockdowns" that harmed the state's economy and personal freedoms . 
* **Election Administration:** The court's decisions during the 2020 election, particularly those regarding mail-in ballots and drop boxes, were characterized by Republicans as creating "election chaos" and undermining election integrity . 
* **Soft on Crime:** Some opposition ads attempted to portray the justices as lenient on criminal defendants, a standard tactic in judicial elections, although this was secondary to the structural arguments about power and overreach .

The **Republican State Leadership Committee (RSLC)** and the **Commonwealth Leaders Fund** (associated with conservative mega-donor Jeff Yass) were the primary financial engines behind this message . They utilized digital advertising, direct mail, and text messaging to urge a "No" vote .

### 4.3. The "Vote Yes" Campaign (Pro-Retention)
The incumbents and their allies countered with a campaign focused on judicial independence and rights protection.

* **Reproductive Rights:** In the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court's *Dobbs* decision, Democrats heavily emphasized the state court's role as the final protector of abortion access in Pennsylvania. The "Vote Yes" campaign framed the retention of the three Democratic justices as essential to preventing an abortion ban . TV ads explicitly stated, "We protected access to abortion... even when the powerful came after it" . 
* **Democracy and Voting Rights:** Supporters argued that the court had protected the right to vote against partisan attempts to disenfranchise Pennsylvanians. They framed the court's redistricting and mail-in ballot rulings as victories for fairness and democratic participation . 
* **Labor Support:** Organized labor was a massive pillar of the "Vote Yes" coalition. The **Pennsylvania AFL-CIO**, **Philadelphia Federation of Teachers**, and **SEIU** mobilized their memberships, endorsing the justices as defenders of workers' rights, collective bargaining, and fair wages . 
* **Judicial Integrity:** The campaign also leveraged the "Recommended" ratings from the Bar Association to argue that the opposition was politically motivated and that the justices were highly qualified professionals doing their jobs .

## 5\. Campaign Finance
The 2025 retention election set new records for spending in a Pennsylvania judicial retention contest. Total spending was estimated to exceed **$15 million**, a staggering sum for a race with no named opponents .

### 5.1. Spending Disparity
Democratic and pro-retention groups significantly outspent their conservative counterparts, with estimates suggesting a **4-to-1** advantage for the "Vote Yes" side . This financial dominance allowed the incumbents to define the narrative early and maintain a constant presence on television and digital platforms throughout the fall.

### 5.2. Independent Expenditure Groups
The majority of the spending did not flow through the candidates' own campaign committees but through independent Political Action Committees (PACs).

* **Pennsylvanians for Judicial Fairness (PJF):** This PAC was the primary vehicle for pro-retention spending. Funded heavily by trial lawyers (via the "Committee for a Better Tomorrow") and labor unions (such as the Carpenter's Union and various teacher's unions), PJF spent over **$3.4 million** on ads supporting the justices . Their ads were slickly produced and focused on the themes of abortion rights and independence . 
* **Vote Yes For Fair And Independent Courts:** Another major pro-retention group, spending approximately **$3.58 million**.17 
* **Commonwealth Leaders Fund:** On the opposition side, this PAC, largely funded by billionaire Jeff Yass, spent heavily to attack the justices. While direct spending on retention was reported around **$356,000** in some filings, the broader network's investment in the "Vote No" narrative was substantial . 
* **Citizens for Term Limits:** A conservative group that spent approximately **$1.4 million** opposing the justices .

### 5.3. Candidate Fundraising
While independent groups dominated the airwaves, the justices also raised funds for their own retention committees.

* **Kevin Dougherty:** Was the most prolific fundraiser among the justices, raising over **$2.6 million** and spending nearly the same amount . 
* **Christine Donohue:** Raised approximately **$891,000** and spent roughly **$820,000**.2 
* **David Wecht:** Reported significantly lower direct spending (approx. **$58,000** in some reports), likely relying on the coordinated spend from the other justices and outside groups to carry his message .

The sheer volume of money poured into the race drew criticism from good-government groups like the **Brennan Center for Justice**, which noted that the influx of outside money threatened to erode public confidence in the impartiality of the courts .

## 6\. Election Results
On November 4, 2025, Pennsylvania voters delivered a decisive verdict, voting to retain all three justices by wide margins. The Associated Press called the races shortly before midnight, confirming that the Democratic majority on the court would remain intact .

### 6.1. Statewide Totals
The official results certified by the Department of State showed a remarkable consistency in the vote totals for all three justices.

| Justice | Party (Affiliation) | "Yes" Votes | "Yes" % | "No" Votes | "No" % | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Christine Donohue** | Democrat | 2,231,527 | **61.80%** | 1,379,599 | 38.20% | **Retained** |
| **Kevin M. Dougherty** | Democrat | 2,227,880 | **61.79%** | 1,377,687 | 38.21% | **Retained** |
| **David Wecht** | Democrat | 2,209,781 | **61.46%** | 1,385,673 | 38.54% | **Retained** |

Source: Pennsylvania Department of State Election Returns 2

The tight clustering of the results—with Donohue and Dougherty separated by fewer than 4,000 votes out of 3.6 million cast—indicated that the electorate treated the retention questions as a slate. Voters largely voted "Yes" to all three or "No" to all three, with very little ticket-splitting or individual differentiation .

### 6.2. Voter Turnout
Turnout for the election was approximately **42.45%** of registered voters, a significant increase from the 36.77% turnout observed in the 2023 municipal election . This boost in participation was attributed to the high visibility of the Supreme Court race, as well as competitive local contests in various jurisdictions . Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt praised the administration of the election, noting that audits confirmed the accuracy of the results .

## 7\. Geographic and Demographic Analysis
A granular analysis of the results reveals the evolving political coalition that supported the court's retention. The "Vote Yes" coalition successfully combined the Democratic base in urban centers with a crucial slice of suburban and swing-county voters who may have been alienated by the "Vote No" campaign's perceived extremism or the attack on judicial independence.

### 7.1. Key Swing Counties
The performance of the justices in Pennsylvania's traditional "bellwether" counties was a critical factor in their comfortable victory.

* **Erie County:** Often cited as the state's most important swing county, Erie voted decisively for retention. Justice Donohue received **62.24%** of the vote (45,160 votes), slightly outperforming her statewide average . This result was significant because Erie had been a highly contested battleground in the previous year's presidential election. The strong retention vote suggested that the Democratic judicial brand remained resilient in working-class areas . 
* **Northampton County:** In the Lehigh Valley, another pivotal swing region, the justices also secured robust victories. Justice Donohue received **54,111 "Yes" votes** versus 32,643 "No" votes (approx. 62%) . This mirrored the success of local Democratic candidates in the county, indicating a strong localized turnout operation or a regional shift toward the Democratic coalition in 2025 .

### 7.2. The Urban-Rural Divide
The election results underscored the stark polarization between Pennsylvania's metropolitan areas and its rural interior, a dynamic often referred to as the "T" (the central and northern rural regions).

* **Support Base:** The "Yes" vote was overwhelming in Philadelphia and Allegheny County (Pittsburgh), the state's two largest population centers. It also carried the influential "collar counties" around Philadelphia (Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, and Bucks), where the message of abortion rights and democracy likely resonated with suburban voters . 
* **Opposition Strongholds:** Conversely, the "No" vote dominated in the rural counties. 
 * **Armstrong County:** Voted **64% No** to 36% Yes . 
 * **Bedford County:** Voted **70% No** to 30% Yes . 
 * **Adams County:** Was more competitive but still leaned against retention, with the "No" vote hovering around **51-52%**.26 
* **The "Blue Wall" in the West:** Interestingly, **Beaver County**, a working-class county in Western Pennsylvania that has trended Republican in recent presidential cycles, voted to *retain* the justices with **53-54%** of the vote . This deviation from the presidential trendline suggests that labor union endorsements (strong in Beaver County) may have played a decisive role in peeling off working-class voters from the GOP's "Vote No" coalition.

### 7.3. Comparison to Top-of-Ticket Trends
Analysts noted that the justices performed better in several areas than the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee, Kamala Harris, had performed the previous year . For instance, in Northampton County, the margin for the justices exceeded the presidential margin, suggesting that the "nonpartisan" nature of the retention ballot, combined with the specific issues of judicial independence and labor rights, allowed the justices to cultivate a broader coalition than a typical partisan candidate .

## 8\. Implications
The retention of Justices Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht had profound legal and political consequences for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

### 8.1. Preservation of the Democratic Majority
The most immediate effect was the preservation of the **5–2 Democratic majority** on the Supreme Court. Had any of the justices been defeated, the governor would have been forced to make a temporary appointment, likely leading to a high-stakes confirmation battle in the State Senate and a precarious balance of power on the court . By securing another ten-year term for Dougherty and Wecht (and a two-year extension for Donohue), the Democratic Party ensured that the court would remain a friendly venue for its policy priorities through the end of the decade .

### 8.2. Future Jurisprudence
With the majority secured, the court was expected to continue its trajectory on key issues:

* **Abortion:** The court is anticipated to rule on the challenge to the state's ban on Medicaid funding for abortion, a case highlighted in the retention campaign ads. The retention of the liberal bloc makes a ruling expanding abortion access under the state's Equal Rights Amendment more likely . 
* **Voting Rights:** The court remains the final arbiter on election disputes. With the 2026 gubernatorial and 2028 presidential elections on the horizon, the court's composition ensures that the expansive interpretation of voting access (regarding mail-in ballots and cure procedures) established in 2020 will likely be upheld . 
* **Education Funding:** Following the *William Penn* decision, the court will likely oversee the implementation of the remedy, potentially forcing the legislature to allocate billions in additional funding to poorer school districts—a stance Justice Wecht explicitly supported in his earlier opinions .

### 8.3. Political Aftermath
For the **Pennsylvania Democratic Party** and **Governor Josh Shapiro**, the 2025 election was a significant victory. It demonstrated the party's ability to mobilize its base in an off-year election and to win the messaging war on judicial issues . The results were interpreted as a vote of confidence in the state's Democratic leadership and a rejection of the "culture war" attacks launched by the opposition .

For the **Republican Party**, the failure to unseat even the most controversial justices highlighted the limitations of the "Vote No" strategy. Without a specific scandal to galvinize voter anger (like the 2005 pay raise), displacing an incumbent judge proved to be an insurmountable challenge, even with significant financial investment .

### 8.4. Upcoming Vacancies
Despite the victories, the composition of the court will not remain static. **Justice Christine Donohue** will face mandatory retirement on December 31, 2027, upon reaching the age of 75 . This will create an open seat that will be contested in the partisan election of 2027\. Both parties are expected to view the 2027 race as the next critical battlefront in the war for the court .

During her first term, Donohue authored several significant opinions and was part of the majority in key civil rights cases.
Donohue's supporters highlighted her role in protecting reproductive rights.

Although the court had not yet issued a definitive ruling on the state constitution's protection of abortion rights by 2025, Donohue was featured in advertisements linking her retention to the defense of such rights.
The Pennsylvania Bar Association (PBA) Judicial Evaluation Commission recommended Christine Donohue for retention.
The PBA described Christine Donohue as "thorough and well-prepared for oral arguments," "smart and fair," and "attentive and engaged."
Under Pennsylvania law, judges must retire at the end of the calendar year in which they turn 75.
Christine Donohue was expected to reach this mandatory retirement age in 2027.
Christine Donohue's retention vote in 2025 was effectively for a two-year extension rather than a full decade.
Christine Donohue's age was noted by political observers but did not become a central theme of the opposition campaign.
Before 2015, Kevin M. Dougherty was the Administrative Judge of the Family Division of the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas.
Kevin M. Dougherty was widely known in state politics not only for his judicial service but also for his family.

Kevin M. Dougherty is the brother of John "Johnny Doc" Dougherty, a prominent and powerful Philadelphia labor leader who was convicted on federal corruption charges in the years preceding the 2025 election.
Despite his brother's legal troubles, Justice Dougherty successfully maintained a distinct professional identity.
Justice Dougherty was not implicated in his brother's activities, and he continued to receive broad support from the legal community and labor unions.
Justice Dougherty's son, Sean Dougherty, also served as a member of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, further cementing the family's political footprint.
The PBA recommended Dougherty for retention.
Attorneys described Justice Dougherty as "attentive, smart, well prepared" and "open to consideration of differing perspectives."
Justice Dougherty's background in family court often informed his perspective on cases involving juvenile justice and social services.
Dougherty was a robust fundraiser, raising over $2.6 million for his retention committee—significantly more than his colleagues.
David N. Wecht served on the Pennsylvania Superior Court before joining the Supreme Court.
David N. Wecht is the son of the famous forensic pathologist Cyril Wecht, a connection that gave him high name recognition in Western Pennsylvania.
Wecht is known for his scholarly, lengthy, and often forceful opinions.
Justice Wecht frequently writes concurrences or dissents that explore the historical and theoretical underpinnings of the law.
One of Justice Wecht's most notable contributions was in the realm of education funding.

Justice Wecht authored a majority opinion asserting that petitioners had the right to challenge the state's education funding formula under the constitution, a ruling that paved the way for the landmark *William Penn* decision which declared the state's school funding system unconstitutional.

Because of his outspoken nature and his authorship of key opinions regarding election administration (such as the extension of mail-in ballot deadlines in 2020), Wecht was a primary target for conservative opposition groups.
The "Vote No" campaigns frequently featured Justice Wecht's image and cited his rulings as examples of "judicial overreach."
Despite the partisan attacks, the PBA highly recommended Justice Wecht.
The PBA stated Justice Wecht's opinions were "well written and logical" and his judicial temperament "above reproach."
The 2025 retention election transformed into a high-stakes political battleground, deviating from the norm of quiet judicial confirmations.
The campaign environment was shaped by the broader national polarization surrounding the judiciary and specific grievances regarding Pennsylvania state policy.
Observers noted that the 2025 cycle was one of the most politicized retention elections in memory.
While the ballot itself remained nonpartisan, the external campaign environment was deeply partisan.

The structural reality of the court—a 5-2 Democratic majority—meant that the retention election was the only mechanism available to Republicans to disrupt Democratic control before the next scheduled open-seat election.
Conservative groups and the Republican Party infrastructure coalesced around a "Vote No" message.
The core argument of the "Vote No" campaign was that Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht had acted as "super-legislators" rather than impartial jurists.
Opponents cited the court's 2018 decision to strike down the GOP-drawn congressional map as an unconstitutional gerrymander, arguing that the court had usurped the legislature's role.
The opposition highlighted the court's rulings that upheld Governor Tom Wolf's emergency powers during the pandemic, including business closures and mask mandates.
These decisions were framed as "lockdowns" that harmed the state's economy and personal freedoms.

The court's decisions during the 2020 election, particularly those regarding mail-in ballots and drop boxes, were characterized by Republicans as creating "election chaos" and undermining election integrity.

Some opposition ads attempted to portray the justices as lenient on criminal defendants, a standard tactic in judicial elections, although this was secondary to the structural arguments about power and overreach.
The Republican State Leadership Committee (RSLC) and the Commonwealth Leaders Fund (associated with conservative mega-donor Jeff Yass) were the primary financial engines behind this message.
They utilized digital advertising, direct mail, and text messaging to urge a "No" vote.
The incumbents and their allies countered with a campaign focused on judicial independence and rights protection.
In the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court's *Dobbs* decision, Democrats heavily emphasized the state court's role as the final protector of abortion access in Pennsylvania.
The "Vote Yes" campaign framed the retention of the three Democratic justices as essential to preventing an abortion ban.
TV ads explicitly stated, "We protected access to abortion... even when the powerful came after it."
Supporters argued that the court had protected the right to vote against partisan attempts to disenfranchise Pennsylvanians.
They framed the court's redistricting and mail-in ballot rulings as victories for fairness and democratic participation.
Organized labor was a massive pillar of the "Vote Yes" coalition.
The Pennsylvania AFL-CIO, Philadelphia Federation of Teachers, and SEIU mobilized their memberships, endorsing the justices as defenders of workers' rights, collective bargaining, and fair wages.

The campaign also leveraged the "Recommended" ratings from the Bar Association to argue that the opposition was politically motivated and that the justices were highly qualified professionals doing their jobs.
The 2025 retention election set new records for spending in a Pennsylvania judicial retention contest.
Total spending was estimated to exceed $15 million, a staggering sum for a race with no named opponents.
Democratic and pro-retention groups significantly outspent their conservative counterparts, with estimates suggesting a 4-to-1 advantage for the "Vote Yes" side.
This financial dominance allowed the incumbents to define the narrative early and maintain a constant presence on television and digital platforms throughout the fall.
The majority of the spending did not flow through the candidates' own campaign committees but through independent Political Action Committees (PACs).
Pennsylvanians for Judicial Fairness (PJF) was the primary vehicle for pro-retention spending.
PJF was funded heavily by trial lawyers (via the "Committee for a Better Tomorrow") and labor unions (such as the Carpenter's Union and various teacher's unions).
PJF spent over $3.4 million on ads supporting the justices.
PJF's ads were slickly produced and focused on the themes of abortion rights and independence.
Vote Yes For Fair And Independent Courts was another major pro-retention group, spending approximately $3.58 million.
On the opposition side, the Commonwealth Leaders Fund, largely funded by billionaire Jeff Yass, spent heavily to attack the justices.
While direct spending on retention by the Commonwealth Leaders Fund was reported around $356,000 in some filings, the broader network's investment in the "Vote No" narrative was substantial.
Citizens for Term Limits is a conservative group that spent approximately $1.4 million opposing the justices.
Kevin Dougherty was the most prolific fundraiser among the justices, raising over $2.6 million and spending nearly the same amount.
Christine Donohue raised approximately $891,000 and spent roughly $820,000.
David Wecht reported significantly lower direct spending (approx. $58,000 in some reports), likely relying on the coordinated spend from the other justices and outside groups to carry his message.
The sheer volume of money poured into the race drew criticism from good-government groups like the Brennan Center for Justice.
The Brennan Center for Justice noted that the influx of outside money threatened to erode public confidence in the impartiality of the courts.
On November 4, 2025, Pennsylvania voters delivered a decisive verdict, voting to retain all three justices by wide margins.
The Associated Press called the races shortly before midnight, confirming that the Democratic majority on the court would remain intact.
The official results certified by the Department of State showed a remarkable consistency in the vote totals for all three justices.
Justice Christine Donohue received 2,231,527 "Yes" Votes (61.80%) and 1,379,599 "No" Votes (38.20%), resulting in her retention.
Justice Kevin M. Dougherty received 2,227,880 "Yes" Votes (61.79%) and 1,377,687 "No" Votes (38.21%), resulting in his retention.
Justice David Wecht received 2,209,781 "Yes" Votes (61.46%) and 1,385,673 "No" Votes (38.54%), resulting in his retention.
The tight clustering of the results—with Donohue and Dougherty separated by fewer than 4,000 votes out of 3.6 million cast—indicated that the electorate treated the retention questions as a slate.
Voters largely voted "Yes" to all three or "No" to all three, with very little ticket-splitting or individual differentiation.
Turnout for the election was approximately 42.45% of registered voters, a significant increase from the 36.77% turnout observed in the 2023 municipal election.
This boost in participation was attributed to the high visibility of the Supreme Court race, as well as competitive local contests in various jurisdictions.
Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt praised the administration of the election, noting that audits confirmed the accuracy of the results.
A granular analysis of the results reveals the evolving political coalition that supported the court's retention.

The "Vote Yes" coalition successfully combined the Democratic base in urban centers with a crucial slice of suburban and swing-county voters who may have been alienated by the "Vote No" campaign's perceived extremism or the attack on judicial independence.
The performance of the justices in Pennsylvania's traditional "bellwether" counties was a critical factor in their comfortable victory.
Erie County, often cited as the state's most important swing county, voted decisively for retention.
Justice Donohue received 62.24% of the vote (45,160 votes) in Erie County, slightly outperforming her statewide average.
This result was significant because Erie had been a highly contested battleground in the previous year's presidential election.
The strong retention vote suggested that the Democratic judicial brand remained resilient in working-class areas.
In the Lehigh Valley, another pivotal swing region, the justices also secured robust victories.
Justice Donohue received 54,111 "Yes" votes versus 32,643 "No" votes (approx. 62%) in Northampton County.
This mirrored the success of local Democratic candidates in Northampton County, indicating a strong localized turnout operation or a regional shift toward the Democratic coalition in 2025.

The election results underscored the stark polarization between Pennsylvania's metropolitan areas and its rural interior, a dynamic often referred to as the "T" (the central and northern rural regions).
The "Yes" vote was overwhelming in Philadelphia and Allegheny County (Pittsburgh), the state's two largest population centers.

The "Yes" vote also carried the influential "collar counties" around Philadelphia (Montgomery, Delaware, Chester, and Bucks), where the message of abortion rights and democracy likely resonated with suburban voters.
Conversely, the "No" vote dominated in the rural counties.
Armstrong County voted 64% No to 36% Yes.
Bedford County voted 70% No to 30% Yes.
Adams County was more competitive but still leaned against retention, with the "No" vote hovering around 51-52%.
Beaver County, a working-class county in Western Pennsylvania that has trended Republican in recent presidential cycles, voted to retain the justices with 53-54% of the vote.

This deviation from the presidential trendline suggests that labor union endorsements (strong in Beaver County) may have played a decisive role in peeling off working-class voters from the GOP's "Vote No" coalition.
Analysts noted that the justices performed better in several areas than the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee, Kamala Harris, had performed the previous year.
In Northampton County, the margin for the justices exceeded the presidential margin.

The "nonpartisan" nature of the retention ballot, combined with the specific issues of judicial independence and labor rights, allowed the justices to cultivate a broader coalition than a typical partisan candidate.
The most immediate effect of the retention of Justices Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht was the preservation of the 5–2 Democratic majority on the Supreme Court.

Had any of the justices been defeated, the governor would have been forced to make a temporary appointment, likely leading to a high-stakes confirmation battle in the State Senate and a precarious balance of power on the court.

By securing another ten-year term for Dougherty and Wecht (and a two-year extension for Donohue), the Democratic Party ensured that the court would remain a friendly venue for its policy priorities through the end of the decade.
With the majority secured, the court was expected to continue its trajectory on key issues.
The court is anticipated to rule on the challenge to the state's ban on Medicaid funding for abortion, a case highlighted in the retention campaign ads.
The retention of the liberal bloc makes a ruling expanding abortion access under the state's Equal Rights Amendment more likely.
The court remains the final arbiter on election disputes.

With the 2026 gubernatorial and 2028 presidential elections on the horizon, the court's composition ensures that the expansive interpretation of voting access (regarding mail-in ballots and cure procedures) established in 2020 will likely be upheld.

Following the *William Penn* decision, the court will likely oversee the implementation of the remedy, potentially forcing the legislature to allocate billions in additional funding to poorer school districts—a stance Justice Wecht explicitly supported in his earlier opinions.
For the Pennsylvania Democratic Party and Governor Josh Shapiro, the 2025 election was a significant victory.
It demonstrated the party's ability to mobilize its base in an off-year election and to win the messaging war on judicial issues.
The results were interpreted as a vote of confidence in the state's Democratic leadership and a rejection of the "culture war" attacks launched by the opposition.
For the Republican Party, the failure to unseat even the most controversial justices highlighted the limitations of the "Vote No" strategy.
Without a specific scandal to galvanize voter anger (like the 2005 pay raise), displacing an incumbent judge proved to be an insurmountable challenge, even with significant financial investment.
Despite the victories, the composition of the court will not remain static.
Justice Christine Donohue will face mandatory retirement on December 31, 2027, upon reaching the age of 75.
This will create an open seat that will be contested in the partisan election of 2027.
Both parties are expected to view the 2027 race as the next critical battlefront in the war for the court.

National money starts flowing into critical Pa. Supreme Court retention races
=============================================================================

[by Stephen Caruso of Spotlight PA| Sept. 9, 2025](https://www.spotlightpa.org/authors/stephen-caruso/)

![Image 3: Screenshot of Republican State Leadership Committee ad](https://www.spotlightpa.org/imgproxy/insecure/rt:fill/w:669/h:446/g:ce/el:1/q:75/MjAyNS8wOS8wMW1iLXkxYmotcmUycC00bnAwLnBuZw==.jpeg)

Share: [](mailto:?subject=National%20money%20starts%20flowing%20into%20critical%20Pa.%20Supreme%20Court%20retention%20races&body=Read%20this%20from%20Spotlight%20PA%0a%0aNational%20money%20starts%20flowing%20into%20critical%20Pa.%20Supreme%20Court%20retention%20races%0aThe%20Republican%20State%20Leadership%20Committee%20has%20spent%20at%20least%20%2485K%20on%20digital%20ads%2c%20urging%20viewers%20to%20vote%20%e2%80%9cNo%20in%20November.%e2%80%9d%0a%0ahttps%3a%2f%2fwww.spotlightpa.org%2fnews%2f2025%2f09%2fpennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election%2f "Share this page by email")[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/feed?app_id=589296315209793&display=page&link=https%3a%2f%2fwww.spotlightpa.org%2fnews%2f2025%2f09%2fpennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election%2f "Share this page on Facebook")[](https://bsky.app/intent/compose?text=National%20money%20starts%20flowing%20into%20critical%20Pa.%20Supreme%20Court%20retention%20races%20https%3a%2f%2fwww.spotlightpa.org%2fnews%2f2025%2f09%2fpennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election%2f "Share this page on Bluesky")[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=National%20money%20starts%20flowing%20into%20critical%20Pa.%20Supreme%20Court%20retention%20races&via=SpotlightPA&url=https%3a%2f%2fwww.spotlightpa.org%2fnews%2f2025%2f09%2fpennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election%2f&tw_p=tweetbutton "Tweet about this page")[](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https%3a%2f%2fwww.spotlightpa.org%2fnews%2f2025%2f09%2fpennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election%2f&title=National%20money%20starts%20flowing%20into%20critical%20Pa.%20Supreme%20Court%20retention%20races "Share on Reddit")

HARRISBURG — A national political group is spending tens of thousands of dollars to urge voters to reject new terms for three Pennsylvania Supreme Court justices. The outcomes of these yes-or-no retention elections could open a path to flip the court from Democratic control.

The Republican State Leadership Committee (RSLC), which helps fund state-level GOP candidates, has spent at least $85,000 on digital ads through Meta and Google as of Sept. 8. These [ads](https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=658302276542345&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&view_all_page_id=50576707351)[ask](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sq1B_2QJ2Tc&ab_channel=RepublicanStateLeadershipCommittee) viewers to vote “No in November,” request a mail ballot, and stop “radical liberal judges” from securing “another decade of power.”

“This is a political consultant's dream, because your message is just one thing, and that's ‘No,’” GOP political consultant Christopher Nicholas [previously](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/02/judicial-retention-election-pennsylvania-2025-supreme-court-partisan/) told Spotlight PA.

Stay informed
-------------

Discover overlooked stories, unique investigations, and daily joy from across PA with our free daily newsletter.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Email address

Sign Up

Retention elections are usually sleepy affairs in which judges handily win new terms. Just one statewide judge has lost — Supreme Court Justice Russell Nigro in 2005 amid widespread grassroots discontent with state government.

The justices asking for additional terms — Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht — were elected as Democrats in 2015, helping flip the court from Republican control. The court’s new liberal majority has ruled on high-profile issues including mail ballots, redistricting, and pandemic-related health measures.

The Pennsylvania Bar Association, a nonpartisan trade group for lawyers that often evaluates judicial candidates’ qualifications, has [recommended](https://pavotesmart.org/current-judicial-ratings/) all three for new terms.

But the Republican Party and groups that support it are highlighting rulings on “COVID lockdowns” and “election chaos” in an effort to defeat them, while also framing these races as a way to support President Donald Trump’s agenda.

Shanin Specter, a Philadelphia trial lawyer and donor to candidates from both major parties, told Spotlight PA that Republicans' push to politicize retention elections would lead justices to start “looking over their shoulders” as they try to interpret the law.

“I've been through a lot of retention elections … and I've never seen an effort like this before, and it calls into question whether our right to impartial justice is going to be upheld,” said Specter, who is the son of the late U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter.

If a justice loses their retention race this November, they must vacate their seat at the end of the year. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro would be able to appoint a temporary justice, but that person would need approval from the state Senate, which is currently controlled by Republicans.

That means any vacant seats are likely to stay that way until after the judicial election in 2027.

Spending in this year’s election is just beginning to emerge. Campaign finance reports, out later this month, will more comprehensively detail spending by political parties, super PACs, and other special interest groups and billionaires.

In a statement, Mason Di Palma, communications director for the RSLC, said that defeating the three justices would “spur a seismic momentum shift in Pennsylvania that would create an opening for more conservative policy victories in the state.”

While You’re Here
-----------------

Spotlight PA’s nonprofit reporting is a free public service, but it depends on your support. Give now to ensure it can continue.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Contribute →](https://www.spotlightpa.org/donate/)

RSLC is financed by traditional GOP donors, including energy companies, banks, business trade groups, and advocates for alternatives to public schools.

“The stakes are high and we know this will be an uphill battle, which is why it's essential that more conservatives get engaged in this fight down the stretch,” he added.

Flipping the court is not as simple as successfully getting voters to pick “no” this fall.

Republicans need at least two Supreme Court seats to be on the 2027 ballot. At least one will be, regardless of the outcome this November. Donohue, one of the justices up for retention in 2025, will face mandatory retirement in 2027 because of her age.

1.title: Election 2025: Pennsylvania Judicial Retention
1.description: Election Outcome and Historical Significance On Nov. 4, 2025, Pennsylvania voters faced a high-stakes statewide ballot: a simple yes/no vote on whether three…
1.content:
**Election Outcome and Historical Significance**

On Nov. 4, 2025, Pennsylvania voters faced a high-stakes statewide ballot: a simple yes/no vote on whether three incumbent justices of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court would be retained for another 10-year term. The justices up for retention were Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty and David Wecht,all of whom had been originally elected as Democrats.

The results showed all three justices retained by large margins, preserving the court’s 5-to-2 Democratic majority.According to preliminary official tallies, each justice secured “Yes” votes in the roughly 60%range,for example, one source lists about 61.4% “Yes” for Donohue.

The retention of all three justices is historically significant. Retention elections in Pennsylvania rarely draw national attention, yet this cycle featured unprecedented spending,estimated at over $15 million, with Democrats outspending Republicans by approximately 4-to-1. If any justice had been voted out, the court’s balance could have shifted, potentially changing the state’s judicial trajectory around redistricting, voting rights and abortion policy.

**Campaign Dynamics and Voter Motivation**

What makes this retention vote especially notable is that, while technically nonpartisan,it was one of the most politicized judicial contests in recent memory. Conservative groups, backed in part by national Republican interests, targeted the three justices with “Vote No” campaigns, calling them too liberal and citing past decisions such as the court’s rejection of a GOP-drawn congressional map.

On the other side, Democrats mobilized aggressively, framing the retention vote as a referendum on protecting abortion rights, preserving the integrity of elections and resisting what they portrayed as partisan efforts to reshape the judiciary. The campaigns emphasized the stakes: the court had the power to rule on redistricting and voting rights cases that could affect the 2026 and 2028 elections. Preelection polling found a relatively high undecided rate;about half of likely voters were undecided on retention just weeks before Election Day.

**Voter Behavior and Geographic Breakdown**

While detailed officials continue certifying county-by-county breakdowns, observers noted increased turnout in suburban and moderate areas where voters appeared motivated by concerns of an overtly political judiciary.Some voters reported choosing “Yes” in part as a rebuke of efforts to remove the justices. The large margins suggest that the pro-retention campaign effectively built a coalition that included labor unions, progressive organizations and younger voters who responded to messaging about rights and representation.

**Policy and Institutional Implications**

The results carry major implications for the judge-driven legal terrain in Pennsylvania. With the status quo maintained, the court will continue at five Democrats to two Republicans, ensuring continuity on decisions involving electoral maps, voting procedure disputes, abortion rights under state law and challenges to state legislation.

In the short term, this outcome means that any attempt by a Republican legislature (or future governor) to push a new congressional map or tighten voting laws will likely face a court still dominated by justices elected as Democrats. In the longer term, the ruling keeps the same ideological makeup of the court heading into the 2026 and 2028 cycles, preserving the Democratic majority at least through those years.

**Political Dynamics and What it Means for 2026-27**

For Republicans, the defeat signifies that, despite heavy investment and an aggressive campaign, it remains difficult to oust incumbent justices in Pennsylvania,even when the election becomes partisan.Some GOP strategists privately voiced concern that the party’s aggressive campaign of “Vote No” may have galvanized turnout among Democrats and moderates who viewed the campaign as an attack on judicial independence.

For Democrats, this victory brings relief and time. Had they lost even one justice, the governor would have had the power to appoint a temporary replacement,and the court’s balance could have affected post-2026 redistricting and voting rights battles. Now, the party can focus its efforts on governance and public policy, while treating the next open seat in 2027 as a strategic priority.

**Risks and What to Watch**

Despite the success,several challenges remain:

*   **Perception of politicization**: The partisan nature of the judicial retention ballot risks eroding public trust in the court’s independence. Future campaigns may further politicize the process.

*   **Coalition shifting**: If voters hold the justices accountable for rulings perceived as controversial (on criminal justice, property rights or election law), future retention fights might be more competitive.

*   **Operational pressure**: The court already faces major caseloads tied to redistricting after the 2026 election. The public will pressure the retained justices to deliver timely, rigorous decisions while managing heightened public scrutiny.

**The Bottom Line**

Pennsylvania’s 2025 Supreme Court retention vote represents a quietly seismic moment for the state’s governance. Voters affirmed the three sitting Democratic affiliated justices, allowing the court’s 5-to-2 liberal majority to persist and ensure continuity in one of the nation’s most pivotal judicial arenas. In doing so, the electorate signaled that they pay attention to institutions that regulate elections,rights and representation and remain willing to engage in what many once saw as low-profile ballots.

7.title: PA Supreme Court mailer uses misleading redistricting claims
7.description: The PAC behind the misleading mailer is part of a network connected to PA's richest person. The goal: convince voters to reject new terms for three PA Supreme Court justices.
7.content:
HARRISBURG — A conservative political action committee is behind a mailer, described by one good-government advocate as “incredibly dishonest,” that urges voters to reject new terms for three state Supreme Court justices.

The PAC is closely connected to two other groups that have been highly visible in the fight to influence the Nov. 4 retention elections. All three are affiliated with GOP heavyweight Matt Brouillette, whose PACs [are mostly funded by](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/12/pennsylvania-election-top-donors-pacs-attorney-general-jeff-yass-state-house/#:~:text=During%20this%20election%20cycle%2C%20Commonwealth,34%20million%20%E2%80%94%20came%20from%20Yass.) Jeff Yass, Pennsylvania’s richest man.

The retention elections — in which [voters will decide whether Justices Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/supreme-court-retention-election-2025-pennsylvania-donohue-dougherty-wecht-elections/) get more time on the bench — are seen as critical in Republican circles.

The court flipped to Democratic control after the 2015 election, and has made [dozens of high-profile decisions](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/judicial-retention-supreme-court-2025-guide-elections/#:~:text=What%20is%20this%20election%20about%3F) over the past decade that have shaped politics and policy. This year marks Republicans’ first real chance to launch a takeover. Their goal is to create vacancies so that they can run competitive, partisan elections in 2027.

That misleading mailer, which began arriving at voters’ homes this month, says that the “liberal Supreme Court gerrymandered our congressional districts to help Democrats win.”

It includes an image of a congressional map, with two of its more convoluted-looking districts circled in red. One, hammer-shaped, stretches more than 100 miles from Pennsylvania’s western border into Cambria and Somerset Counties. The other, even more jagged, sprawls from Lackawanna County down to Pine Grove, in southern Schuylkill County.

But that’s not a map the current court drew.

In fact, a GOP-controlled state legislature drew it in 2011. The current court overturned it in 2018, declaring it a partisan gerrymander that favored Republicans.

That 2011 map was the impetus for Carol Kuniholm, who advocates for nonpartisan reapportionment with the group Fair Districts PA, to get involved in the politics of redistricting. Despite Democrats having a voter registration edge in the commonwealth, under that map, Republicans had won 13 of Pennsylvania’s 18 congressional seats three elections in a row. So the court’s decision to overturn it, Kuniholm said, was a watershed.

She’s been involved in redistricting advocacy ever since, and has seen a lot of contentious judicial races. But of the mailer she called “dishonest,” she noted, “I don't think anybody has seen anything like this.”

Voters have noticed the mailer too.

Bill Litvin, of Berks County, received it. Litvin is a registered Republican, and he’s deeply familiar with congressional maps because he’s also a member of the League of Women Voters, which advocates for fair redistricting and other election-related issues.

Litvin immediately knew the map in the ad wasn’t the current congressional map. But other voters, he noted, might not.

“It would just be nice if all the participants in the election would be honest. It turns a lot of people off from voting when they aren’t,” he told Spotlight PA.

Who is funding the mailers?
---------------------------

The mailers in question are being funded by Commonwealth Leaders Fund. It is one of two PACs administered by the conservative nonprofit Commonwealth Partners, which Brouillette runs. Thanks to Yass’ money, the group is a central player in funding and promoting virtually all high-profile Republican candidates in Pennsylvania races, from the state House to the governorship.

Commonwealth Leaders’ relationship to Yass is well-established.

Last year, in the lead-up to the presidential election, Commonwealth Leaders received more than $18.5 million from another PAC run by Commonwealth Partners called Commonwealth Children’s Choice Fund. That PAC had received the vast majority of its funding directly from another PAC, Students First, which is exclusively funded by Yass.

Commonwealth Partners has also paid directly for mailers that urge voters to term-limit the court’s justices, as well as ones that invoke high-profile sexual abuse cases on which the court ruled.

![Image 1: Three mailers paid for by Commonwealth Partners seeking to sway voters in upcoming retention elections.](https://www.spotlightpa.org/imgproxy/insecure/rt:fill/w:669/h:446/g:sm/el:1/q:75/MjAyNS8wOS8wMW1kLW55a3AtZmNtZi1zM3NmLmpwZWc=.jpeg)

Three mailers paid for by Commonwealth Partners seeking to sway voters in upcoming retention elections.(Sarah Anne Hughes / Spotlight PA)

Then there’s a new nonprofit, Citizens for Term Limits, which was established in May and registered with the state at the same Harrisburg address as Commonwealth Partners’ office. It [has a website](https://www.citizensfortermlimits.net/), and in just the past week, has made [at least $17,900 in ad buys on Meta social media platforms](https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=political_and_issue_ads&country=US&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&view_all_page_id=754200141109589). Spotlight PA has also viewed text message advertising funded by the nonprofit.

Uncovering how much each group is spending on these elections is difficult. Commonwealth Leaders Fund must file regular campaign finance reports with the state. In its most recent report, which covers June 10 to Sept. 15, it reported spending more than $37,600 on “direct mail.”

It’s even harder to track spending from the two nonprofits, which are generally not required to disclose their donors and do not file campaign finance reports.

Individuals and companies that spend on political races in Pennsylvania without coordinating with a particular campaign often report their spending as “independent expenditures,” which at least tells voters how much they paid to influence the race. However, neither Commonwealth Partners nor Citizens for Term Limits has so far reported any independent expenditures.

A spokesperson for Commonwealth Partners told Spotlight PA that “All appropriate expenditures are reported accurately and on time.” They did not comment on the redistricting ad.

The real history of the map in that mailer
------------------------------------------

The Pennsylvania Supreme Court, which currently has a 5-2 majority of judges elected as Democrats, has been heavily involved in redistricting in recent years.

In 2011, the then-Republican-controlled General Assembly and Republican governor passed a congressional map under which GOP candidates won all but five of Pennsylvania’s 18 seats for three elections in a row.

That changed in 2018. A group of Democratic voters had sued the state, arguing that the 2011 map was gerrymandered to favor Republicans and effectively disenfranchised them. The state Supreme Court ruled in their favor, writing that the map “clearly, plainly and palpably” violated the state constitution and the legislature should redraw it in time for that year’s primary election.

The high court’s decision was mostly partisan — one Democratic justice disagreed with the speed of the timeline for implementing a new map —though a Republican Commonwealth Court judge [did note in a finding of fact on the case](https://pubintlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/17.12.29-Recommended-Findings-of-Fact-and-Conclusions-of-Law.pdf) “that partisan considerations are evident in the enacted 2011 Plan, such that the 2011 Plan overall favors Republican Party candidates in certain congressional districts.”

That judge was Kevin Brobson, who now sits on the state Supreme Court.

After state lawmakers were unable to agree on a redrawn congressional map, the state Supreme Court justices commissioned one themselves. That map yielded a 9-9 partisan split in the next congressional election.

A similar process played out in 2021, the next time the map underwent its usual redraw. The legislature and governor again deadlocked, and the court again commissioned and selected a map — opting for one that skewed close to their 2018 pick.

These days, Republicans again have an upper hand within Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation, with 10 members to Democrats’ seven. (The state lost a congressional seat in the last redistricting cycle.)

Kuniholm noted that the state constitution promises Pennsylvanians free and equal elections, and she considers it “incredibly important for Pennsylvania that we have a court that takes our rights seriously” when it comes to redistricting.

“Clearly,” she added, “the ones who had drawn the gerrymandered map are not happy.”

"Share on Reddit")

HARRISBURG — Spending has officially begun on both sides of Pennsylvania’s 2025 Supreme Court election, which will task voters with retaining or rejecting three justices.

A political group funded by a mix of state and national Democratic donors has begun running at least one TV ad in favor of new 10-year terms for the three justices. Christine Donohue, Kevin Dougherty, and David Wecht were all elected as Democrats in 2015.

The ad, paid for by Pennsylvanians for Judicial Fairness — or PJF — asks voters to vote yes and “keep the Supreme Court independent.”

The ad also highlights a case, brought by a handful of reproductive health providers, that argues the state constitution [protects access to abortion](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/08/pennsylvania-supreme-commonwealth-court-abortion-climate-change-guns/). While the high court has [yet to rule on the case's merits](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2024/01/pennsylvania-abortion-rights-supreme-court-constitution-guarantee-ruling-commonwealth-court/), it tossed out a lower court’s ruling.

“Vote and protect your rights,” the ad concludes.

Sign Up

A representative for PJF did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The message counters ads by a national Republican group that’s put [at least $85,000 into the opposite message](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2025/09/pennsylvania-supreme-court-retention-election-republican-campaign-election/) — a no vote.. As Spotlight PA reported last week, those [ads](https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=658302276542345&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&view_all_page_id=50576707351)[include](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sq1B_2QJ2Tc&ab_channel=RepublicanStateLeadershipCommittee) a call to stop “radical liberal judges” from securing “another decade of power.”

The stakes of this retention election are high for both groups.

Since voters put Donohue, Dougherty, and Wecht on the bench nearly a decade ago, flipping the court from GOP control, the Democratic majority has ruled on high-profile issues including mail ballots, redistricting, and pandemic-related health measures.

The Pennsylvania Bar Association, a nonpartisan trade group for lawyers that often evaluates judicial candidates’ qualifications, has [recommended](https://pavotesmart.org/current-judicial-ratings/) all three justices for new terms.

PFJ, the pro-retention group, has not yet been required to file a campaign finance report this year, so it is unclear how much it has raised or spent on ads or other political actions. But the same group spent millions during the contested 2023 state Supreme Court race in favor of Democrat and eventual winner Justice Daniel McCaffery.

That year, the PAC [received](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2023/11/pennsylvania-election-results-abortion-supreme-court-spending/) big checks from organized labor and trial lawyers as well as from out-of-state billionaires who have a history of donating to pro-abortion-access causes. It also got funding from a handful of “dark money” groups that do not disclose donors.

Retention elections are usually sleepy affairs in which judges handily win new terms. Just one statewide judge has ever lost — Supreme Court Justice Russell Nigro in 2005, amid widespread grassroots discontent with state government.

If a justice loses their retention race this November, they must vacate their seat at the end of the year. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro would be able to appoint a temporary justice, but that person would need approval from the state Senate, which is currently controlled by Republicans.

The GOP needs at least two Supreme Court seats to be on the 2027 ballot in order to have a hope of taking back control. At least one will be, regardless of the outcome this November. Donohue, one of the justices up for retention in 2025, will face mandatory retirement in 2027 because of her age.

Election Day is Nov. 4.

2.content:
[![Image 1: This is a good article. Click here for more information.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/94/Symbol_support_vote.svg/20px-Symbol_support_vote.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Good_articles* "This is a good article. Click here for more information.")

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

2025 Pennsylvania Supreme Court retention election![Image 2: A 60x44 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Flag_of_Pennsylvania.svg/60px-Flag_of_Pennsylvania.svg.png)

* * *
